desc:
A courier travels across an m x n grid from the top-left cell (0, 0) to the bottom-right cell (m-1, n-1), moving one step right or one step down at a time. All cells (r, c) with r1 ≤ r ≤ r2 and c1 ≤ c ≤ c2 form a flooded rectangle that must not be entered. The rectangle never contains the start or the destination cell.

Return the number of routes that avoid the rectangle, modulo 1,000,000,007. The grid is far too large to fill cell by cell.

m = 3, n = 3, rectangle rows 1..1, columns 1..1  ->  2
m = 3, n = 3, rectangle rows 1..1, columns 0..2  ->  0
m = 2, n = 5, rectangle rows 0..0, columns 2..3  ->  2
constraints: 0 ≤ r1 ≤ r2 < m and 0 ≤ c1 ≤ c2 < n
The rectangle contains neither (0, 0) nor (m-1, n-1)
hints: Counting all routes is one binomial coefficient: C(m+n-2, m-1). Maybe it is easier to count the routes that do touch the rectangle and subtract.
Every route that touches the rectangle has a unique first cell inside it, and that cell is either on the top edge (entered from above) or on the left edge (entered from the left).

For each entry cell multiply (routes from the start to the cell just before it) by (routes from the entry cell to the destination). Both factors are binomials, so the total is O(m + n) terms. Precompute factorials and inverse factorials modulo the prime.
editorial: Routes avoiding the rectangle = all routes minus routes that touch it. A route that touches the rectangle enters it for the first time at exactly one cell. That cell is either in the top row of the rectangle (r = r1, columns c1..c2) and was entered from the cell above, or in its left column (c = c1, rows r1..r2) and was entered from the cell to its left. The cell (r1, c1) is allowed to be entered from both sides, and these two situations are different routes, so nothing is double counted.

Nothing before the entry touches the rectangle: the cell above a top-edge entry lies in row r1-1 and the cell to the left of a left-edge entry lies in column c1-1, so any route to it is automatically clear. Hence the number of bad routes through the top edge is the sum over c of W(0,0 -> r1-1,c) · W(r1,c -> m-1,n-1) (only if r1 > 0), and similarly for the left edge, where W(a,b -> x,y) = C((x-a)+(y-b), x-a). With factorial tables modulo the prime the whole answer takes O(m + n) time.
